summary: Specifies how RADIUS operates over IPv6 and defines the RADIUS attributes used for IPv6 network access.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3162 adds RADIUS fields for IPv6 network access. A RADIUS server can send a network access server an IPv6 address, prefix, route, or related setting.

questions: which radius attribute numbers are used for ipv6
subtitle: RADIUS attributes carry IPv6 addresses, prefixes, routes, and related access settings.

tldr.problem: RADIUS could authenticate and configure network access, but it lacked fields for IPv6 addresses, interface identifiers, prefixes, and routes.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3162 defines six IPv6 RADIUS attributes numbered 95 through 100 and describes using RADIUS over IPv4 or IPv6 transport.
tldr.outcome: A RADIUS server can provide IPv6 configuration information to a network access server. RFC 3162 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 8044.

today: RFC 3162 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2001. It has been updated by RFC 8044 and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: RADIUS for IPv6 Access
sections.content:
RADIUS can run over IPv6 and can carry attributes used to configure IPv6 network access. When a network access server (NAS) asks a RADIUS server to authenticate a user, it may not yet know whether the host will use IPv4, IPv6, or both.

The NAS may therefore receive IPv4 and IPv6 attributes together and choose the settings the client can use. The access method, such as native IPv6 or an IPv6 tunnel, does not change RADIUS operation itself.
sections.plainLanguage: The NAS may not know which address type a user will use when it asks RADIUS for access settings. It can receive IPv4 and IPv6 information, then use the suitable settings.

sections.title: Addresses, Interface IDs, and Prefixes
sections.content:
NAS-IPv6-Address (type 95) identifies the NAS with a 16-octet IPv6 address and appears only in Access-Request packets. Framed-Interface-Id (type 96) carries an 8-octet interface identifier for the user. A NAS may include the identifier as a hint after negotiating the IPv6CP Interface-Identifier option.

Framed-IPv6-Prefix (type 97) supplies a prefix and its route for the user. It may appear more than once in an Access-Accept, and in an Access-Request it is only a hint. Its length is 4 to 20 octets; its prefix length is 0 to 128 bits, and unused prefix bits must be zero.
sections.plainLanguage: These attributes identify the NAS, suggest an interface identifier, or give the user an IPv6 prefix. The server can send a prefix as a setting or consider it as a request hint.

sections.title: Login Hosts, Routes, and Prefix Pools
sections.content:
Login-IPv6-Host (type 98) names the host the NAS should connect the user to when Login-Service is present. An all-ones address means the user may choose a host; zero means the NAS should choose one. Framed-IPv6-Route (type 99) carries text describing a route to configure for the user.

Framed-IPv6-Pool (type 100) names an IPv6 prefix pool configured on the NAS. The NAS should use it to assign a prefix, and must ignore the attribute if it does not support multiple prefix pools.
sections.plainLanguage: Other attributes can name a login host, describe a route, or select a prefix pool. A NAS that cannot use multiple pools ignores the pool attribute.

sections.title: Where the Attributes May Appear
sections.content:
The RFC's table states which packet types may carry each attribute and how many copies are allowed. NAS-IPv6-Address is limited to one in an Access-Request or Accounting-Request. Framed-IPv6-Route may appear several times in an Access-Accept, while Framed-IPv6-Pool is limited to one there.

None of the six IPv6 attributes may appear in Access-Reject or Access-Challenge packets. The table also identifies which attributes can occur in Accounting-Request packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Each attribute has rules for which RADIUS packet may carry it and how many copies are allowed. The packet-type table defines these limits for requests, replies, and accounting.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This RFC describes RADIUS use in IPv6-enabled networks; RADIUS may travel over IPv4 or IPv6. The document points to existing RADIUS security concerns. It notes that IPsec is mandatory to implement for IPv6 and expects IPv6-capable RADIUS implementations typically to use IPsec.

A RADIUS shared secret protects password attributes and helps provide confidentiality, integrity, and authentication. Only IPsec ESP with a non-null transform can replace that application-layer protection. With AH or null ESP, a shared secret will typically still be needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing the network to IPv6 does not remove RADIUS security needs. The RFC explains when IPsec can provide the protection that a RADIUS shared secret normally supplies.

sections.title: The Six Attribute Numbers
sections.content: The RFC requests six new RADIUS attribute numbers: NAS-IPv6-Address, Framed-Interface-Id, Framed-IPv6-Prefix, Login-IPv6-Host, Framed-IPv6-Route, and Framed-IPv6-Pool. Their assigned numbers are listed in the attribute table as 95 through 100.
sections.plainLanguage: The six new IPv6 attributes each receive a number in the RADIUS attribute list. Their numbers run from 95 through 100.

viz.caption: The six RADIUS attributes for IPv6

items.label: NAS-IPv6-Address
items.desc: Identifies the NAS in an Access-Request.

items.label: Framed-IPv6-Prefix
items.desc: Supplies a prefix and its route.

items.label: Login-IPv6-Host
items.desc: Names a host for the user to access.

items.label: Framed-IPv6-Route
items.desc: Provides routing information for the user.

items.label: Framed-IPv6-Pool
items.desc: Names a prefix pool on the NAS.
